slides.title: Supporting Your Middle Schooler's Reading at Home
slides.subtitle: A twelve-minute routine that fits a real weeknight
slides.notes:
Open by naming the room's actual problem: most parents here have already tried telling their child to read more, and it did not work. Say that out loud in the first thirty seconds. It buys you the rest of the talk.

Set expectations: twelve minutes, four nights a week, and you are not going to ask anyone to buy anything or become a reading teacher.

Introduce yourself in one sentence. Do not spend three minutes on your background; they came for the routine.

slides.title: The Twelve-Minute Routine
bullets: Four nights a week. Not seven.
Three minutes: they read aloud to you.
Six minutes: they read silently, you sit nearby.
Three minutes: you ask one question.
slides.notes:
The number that matters here is four, not twelve. A routine that happens four nights beats a longer one that collapses by Wednesday. Say explicitly that missing nights is built into the plan, because a parent who thinks they failed on night three usually stops entirely.

Reading aloud first does two things: it tells you whether the words themselves are hard, and it warms them up before silent reading.

Sitting nearby during the silent stretch matters more than it sounds. You are not supervising. You are making reading a thing that happens in company rather than a punishment served alone in a bedroom.

If a parent asks what the child should read: anything they will actually finish. Graphic novels count. Sports articles count. This is not the fight to pick tonight.

Frame this as practice guidance drawn from classroom experience, not as a research finding. If someone asks for the evidence base, point them to the resources on the last slide and say honestly that this is a routine that works for many families, not a studied intervention.

slides.title: What It Looks Like: Marcus, Grade 7
bullets: Reads the words accurately. Remembers almost nothing.
Avoids reading by starting an argument about reading.
What worked was not more minutes.
It was one question, asked before he started.
slides.footnote: Marcus is a composite drawn from several students. No real student is described.
slides.notes:
Say clearly, out loud: Marcus is a composite, drawn from several students. No real student is being described. Parents relax when you say this, and it is the honest thing to do.

The argument pattern is the part the room will recognize. A seventh grader who cannot hold what he reads would rather be the kid who refuses than the kid who cannot. Refusing is a choice; failing is not. Name that, and half the room will recognize their own kitchen table.

The question asked before reading was simply: what do you think this is going to be about? Thirty seconds, before page one. It gave him something to confirm or correct, which gave him a reason to hold the thread.

This is the emotional center of the talk. Slow down here. Do not rush to the next slide.

If a parent says 'that is my child' - and someone will - acknowledge it and move on rather than starting a one-on-one consultation in front of forty people. Offer to talk afterward.

slides.title: Three Things to Say
bullets: "What do you think happens next?"
"Show me the part where you got lost."
"Tell me that page in your own words."
slides.notes:
These are the whole toolkit. Three questions, and parents do not need to understand reading instruction to use any of them.

The first one is a prediction. It gives the reader a reason to keep going.

The second is the most useful of the three, and the one parents skip. It assumes getting lost is normal and expected, which makes admitting it safe. A child who can point at the sentence where comprehension broke has just done something genuinely difficult.

The third is retelling. If they cannot retell a page, they did not read it, no matter how accurately the words came out. This is the one that catches the Marcus problem.

Tell parents to pick one and use it all week. Three new habits at once is how this fails. One habit, four nights, is how it works.

If the room is engaged, ask them to try the third question on each other right now with anything on their phone. Thirty seconds. It makes the point better than another slide.

slides.title: Three Things to Skip
bullets: Do not correct every mispronounced word.
Do not turn the twelve minutes into a quiz.
Do not make reading the consequence for a bad grade.
slides.notes:
Every item here is something well-meaning parents do, so deliver it without blame. Say 'this is the one I would have done too' if that is true for you.

Correcting every word interrupts meaning-making. If the mistake does not change the meaning, let it go. If it does, wait until the end of the sentence.

The quiz problem is the most common. A child who knows questions are coming reads to survive the questions, not to understand. One question, after, is a conversation. Six is an interrogation.

The third is the quiet one and worth saying firmly: the moment reading becomes a punishment, you have taught your child what reading is for. That lesson lasts longer than any one bad grade.

Pause after this slide. It is the one parents most often want to ask about.

slides.title: When to Ask the School for More
bullets: Avoiding reading in every subject, not just English.
Grades dropping while effort stays the same.
Rereading one paragraph three times and still not holding it.
slides.footnote: Three questions worth asking: who do I talk to, what do you already know, and what happens next?
slides.notes:
The first three are signals, not diagnoses. Be careful with wording. You are telling parents when a conversation is warranted, not telling them what is wrong with their child.

The cross-subject signal matters most. Reading trouble shows up in science and social studies before anyone calls it a reading problem.

The three questions on the last line are the practical gift of this slide. Many parents do not know they are allowed to ask what information the school already has. They are.

Name the actual starting point at your school - the counselor, the team lead, whoever it genuinely is. If you do not know, say you will find out and follow up, rather than guessing from the front of a room.

Do not use terms like evaluation, tier, or intervention without defining them. If you use one, define it in the same breath.

Say plainly that asking a question is not a referral and does not start a process on its own. Parents who fear setting something irreversible in motion often say nothing for a year.

slides.title: Where to Go Next
bullets: AdLit - adlit.org (grades 4-12, from WETA)
Colorín Colorado - colorincolorado.org (multilingual families)
Improving Literacy - improvingliteracy.org (your state's dyslexia laws)
IES practice guide, grades 4-9 - ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/practiceguide/29
slides.notes:
Keep this slide up while you take questions. People photograph it.

Before presenting, open all four and confirm each one still loads and still covers what this slide claims. This is a blocking item on the quality checklist, and an address that has moved is the kind of small failure a room remembers.

AdLit is the one to point at first. It is WETA's site for grades 4-12, so it is built for the age in this room. Reading Rockets, its better-known sister site, is deliberately not on this list: its focus is PreK through third grade, and sending a seventh grader's parent there wastes their evening.

Colorín Colorado is second. Bilingual, practical, and the right first stop for any family in the room raising a reader in more than one language.

Improving Literacy earns its place for one specific thing: a tool for looking up your own state's dyslexia laws, which is exactly what a parent needs before the conversation on the previous slide. Most of its family material is aimed at much younger children, so point at the state-law tool rather than the site in general.

The IES practice guide is the research base, written for educators rather than parents. Mention it for the parent who asks what the evidence says, and tell them honestly that it is heavy going.

Close by restating the one action: four nights, twelve minutes, one question. Not the whole deck. One action.

If you are handing anything out, this slide is the handout.
